summary: Describes how a single router can share circuits among multiple IS-IS routing protocol instances, isolating resources for each. Each instance forms its own adjacencies and can support multiple topologies, identified by a new TLV. It replaces RFC 6822.

plainLanguage.summary: One building can host several separate clubs that use the same hallway but keep their own books.

questions: multiple is-is instances on one router
what is the iid-tlv in is-is
what is an itid in is-is
does multi-instance is-is work with legacy routers
subtitle: Lets one router run several separate IS-IS routing instances over the same links, each with its own topologies.

tldr.problem: IS-IS as defined in ISO 10589 allows only one protocol instance per circuit and one Link State Database per instance, so resources cannot be isolated and some information is flooded to routers that do not need it.
tldr.mechanism: A new Instance Identifier TLV (type 7) marks every PDU of a non-zero instance with a 16-bit instance ID and, optionally, instance-specific topology IDs. Each instance forms its own adjacencies and each topology gets its own Update Process and LSDB.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 6822, and it relaxes RFC 6822 so that RFC 5120 multi-topology can be used inside a non-zero instance.

today: RFC 8202 is a Proposed Standard. It obsoletes RFC 6822, and no RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Why Multiple Instances
sections.content:
A limitation of the protocol in ISO 10589 is that only one instance of IS-IS can run on a given circuit. Multi-Instance IS-IS (MI-IS-IS) removes it. A router that supports the extension is called a Multi-Instance-capable router (MI-RTR).

Separate instances help isolate resources inside a router and across the network. Each instance can have its own priorities for processing PDUs and its own flooding parameters, so instances can consume network-wide resources at different rates.

A second limitation is that an instance has a single Update Process working on a single Link State Database (LSDB). Non-zero instances may have several Update Processes, each tied to a topology with its own LSDB. Legacy routers use the standard (zero) instance, and its behavior is not changed. Uses include topology-specific routing and carrying information for applications (RFC 6823). Specifying such uses is out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: Normally a hallway can carry only one club's mail system. Now each club can have its own mail room and still share the hallway.

sections.title: The Instance Identifier TLV
sections.content:
An Instance Identifier (IID) names an IS-IS instance, and the new IID-TLV is carried in the PDUs of every non-zero instance: IIHs, SNPs and LSPs. IIDs MUST be unique within the routing domain. IID 0 is reserved for the standard instance, and its PDUs MUST NOT include an IID-TLV except where noted. A PDU without an IID-TLV belongs to the standard instance.

The TLV also lists Instance-specific Topology Identifiers (ITIDs), 16-bit values where all of 0 to 65535 are valid. In an SNP or LSP, exactly one ITID MUST be present, otherwise the PDU MUST be ignored. In an IIH with a non-zero IID, at least one ITID MUST be present, and it lists the ITIDs the circuit supports. A single TLV holds up to 126 ITIDs. If several IID-TLVs appear and their IIDs differ, the PDU MUST be ignored.

ITID 0 is reserved for a special use case and MUST NOT be combined with any non-zero ITID. When an LSP is purged, the IID-TLV MUST be kept and the rest of the body SHOULD be removed. Placing the IID-TLV first in the PDU is recommended.
sections.plainLanguage: Every letter gets a club number stamped on the envelope, plus the names of the topics it is about. Letters with no stamp belong to the original club.

sections.title: Adjacencies and the Update Process
sections.content:
MI-RTRs form instance-specific adjacencies. On a point-to-point circuit, a router that receives an IIH checks the IID-TLV, and if the IID matches one it supports on that circuit it uses the normal procedure to set up an adjacency for that instance. For non-zero instances an adjacency SHOULD NOT be established unless at least one ITID is shared. Point-to-point setup MUST use the three-way handshake of RFC 5303, so a non-MI neighbor cannot bring up an adjacency prematurely.

On a broadcast circuit, a Designated Intermediate System (DIS) is elected per instance, so different instances may have different DISs. The DIS generates pseudo-node LSPs for all supported ITIDs. If the ITID sets of MI-RTRs on one circuit are inconsistent, connectivity for the unsupported topologies can be compromised.

A unique Update Process exists for each supported ITID. On point-to-point circuits it only runs for ITIDs both routers support. When authentication is used, the IID first selects which authentication configuration applies, and the check then proceeds as normal.
sections.plainLanguage: Each club elects its own class monitor, so the monitor of one club need not be the monitor of another.

sections.title: Coexisting with Legacy Routers
sections.content:
A router that does not implement this extension silently ignores the unknown TLV, so every PDU it receives looks like the standard instance. The RFC therefore adds safeguards.

Broadcast circuits: PDUs for a non-zero IID MUST go to one of two new Layer 2 multicast addresses, AllL1MI-ISs or AllL2MI-ISs, which legacy routers do not process. Standard-instance PDUs keep using AllL1IS or AllL2IS. An MI-RTR MUST discard a PDU with an IID-TLV sent to AllL1IS, AllL2IS or AllIS, and a PDU sent to the MI addresses that has no IID-TLV or has IID 0. Misuse would corrupt the LSDB of legacy systems and could cause inconsistent DIS election.

Point-to-point circuits: all IIHs sent by an MI-RTR MUST include an IID-TLV, even for IID 0. The presence or absence of the TLV in a neighbor's IIH shows whether it supports the extension. Once an IIH without an IID-TLV arrives, the MI-RTR MUST NOT send PDUs for any instance other than 0.
sections.plainLanguage: The new clubs use a special mailbox so that the old club never opens a letter meant for someone else and gets confused.

sections.title: Usage Guidelines and M-ISIS
sections.content:
The RFC gives examples but does not constrain implementors. With a one-to-one mapping, one topology is used and its single LSDB is flooded to all MI-RTRs of the instance. With a many-to-one mapping, several ITIDs let each subset of information be flooded only to the routers interested in it, and each ITID can have a full LSP set of 256 LSPs at each level. The topology for each ITID MUST be fully connected for flooding to work. In many cases a single non-zero instance is sufficient and optimal; several instances make sense when the desired topologies of two sets of applications are largely disjoint.

RFC 5120 multi-topology uses 12-bit MTIDs and has no relationship to ITIDs. An MI-RTR MAY run RFC 5120 multi-topology inside a non-zero instance when ITID 0 is supported, and then ITID 0 MUST be the only ITID. It MUST NOT do so when any non-zero ITID is supported, and LSPs with TLV 222, 235 or 237 in that case MUST be ignored. Graceful restart (RFC 5306) applies, but all topology-specific LSP databases must be synchronized, using additional T2 timers.
sections.plainLanguage: You can give each topic its own notebook so people only get the notebooks they care about, instead of everyone reading everything.

sections.title: IANA Registrations and Security
sections.content:
IANA registered TLV 7, Instance Identifier, valid in IIH, LSP, SNP and purge PDUs. Under RFC 6822, IANA also registered two EUI-48 multicast addresses: 01-00-5E-90-00-02 for AllL1MI-ISs and 01-00-5E-90-00-03 for AllL2MI-ISs. References to RFC 6822 in the registries were replaced by this document.

The Security Considerations section adds nothing new and points to ISO 10589, RFC 5304 and RFC 5310 for IS-IS security.
sections.plainLanguage: The official list of numbers and addresses now has entries for the new club stamp and the two special mailboxes.

fields.name: Supported ITID
fields.desc: Repeated for each supported topology; length is 2 to 254 octets overall.
